title: Crocosmia paniculata

{{Short description|Species of flowering plant}} {{About|the plant named Aunt Eliza|the enslaved woman of Sam Houston commonly called Aunt Eliza|Sam Houston and slavery#Eliza Revel}} {{Speciesbox |image = Aunt Eliza (Crocosmia paniculata) red flowers (46724994502).jpg |genus = Crocosmia |species = paniculata |authority = ([[Friedrich Wilhelm Klatt|Klatt]]) [[Peter Goldblatt|Goldblatt]] |synonyms = ''Antholyza paniculata'' Klatt
''Curtonus paniculatus'' (Klatt) N.E.Br. }} '''''Crocosmia paniculata''''' is a bulbous flowering plant that is native to eastern South Africa, [[Lesotho]], and [[Eswatini]], growing in wet areas by streams, marshes, and drainages. Plants reach 4 to 5 ft (1.2–1.5 m) tall, with lanceolate leaves and deep orange to orange-brown flowers. It is a popular ornamental plant.{{cite web|url=http://www.pacificbulbsociety.org/pbswiki/index.php/Crocosmia|title=Crocosmia|publisher=Pacific Bulb Society|access-date=4 September 2012}} The plant has [[escaped plant|escaped cultivation]] and become established in the wild in parts of the [[United Kingdom]].{{Citation| title=Protected Species and Non-Native Species| publisher=Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs| place=London, UK| pages=13| year=2007| url=http://www.defra.gov.uk/wildlife-pets/wildlife/management/non-native/documents/consultation.pdf| format=PDF| access-date=2010-03-01| url-status=dead| archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20101205123933/http://www.defra.gov.uk/wildlife-pets/wildlife/management/non-native/documents/consultation.pdf| archive-date=2010-12-05}} The common name '''Aunt Eliza''' is derived from the former generic name ''Antholyza''.{{cite web|url=http://www.theafricangarden.com/crocosmia_paniculata.html|title=Crocosmia paniculata - Aunt Liza|work=The African Garden|access-date=4 September 2012}} In Lesotho, where it is native, the plant is used by the indigenous [[Sotho people]] as an [[antidiarrhoeal]] remedy, administered not only to humans, but also to cattle so afflicted."Medicinal and Poisonous Plants of Southern and Eastern Africa" Watt J.M. and Breyer-Brandwijk M.G. pub.
